title: Family Anthony B. Bradley Ten Questions to Help Your Son Become the Man He's Meant to Be
author: Bradley, Anthony B.
summary: Bradley writes as a father-theologian making the case that fathers are the most significant and enduring voice in their sons' lives -- more influential than peers, pastors, or social media -- and that summer is a critical window for intentional conversation about who a son is becoming. Drawing on Dr. Karen Horney's psychology of imagination, Bradley argues that whatever a young man imagines about himself over the summer, he will tend to live out -- making it essential that fathers shape that imagination before peers and media do. The piece introduces two worksheet-based guides (one for high schoolers, one for sons leaving for college), structured as ten questions for summer reflection with a begin-of-summer session and an end-of-summer debrief. The key relational posture prescribed for fathers is listening rather than prescribing: the goal is to hear the son's honest heart in a space of safety and non-judgment. Bradley frames the exercise as a 'Special Forces mission' arguing that a father's voice weighs as much as an aircraft carrier in a son's life.
points: * Fathers are the most significant voice in a son's life through adolescence and beyond -- more than peers or youth pastors -- and this influence continues until the father dies; any belief that peer influence overtakes paternal influence in the teenage years is a myth that leads fathers to disengage at precisely the wrong moment. * Imagination shapes destiny: Dr. Karen Horney's research shows that people imagine their futures and then live them out -- for good or ill -- making it imperative that fathers actively shape a son's imagination before summer peers and media do. * The father's posture in these conversations must be listening, not teaching: the son must be given safety to share honestly where he really is, not where he thinks his father wants him to be. * Summer is a specific season of heightened vulnerability and opportunity: the first year after high school is especially critical for faith persistence among church-raised boys, and a father who leans in as guide, coach, and sage changes the trajectory. * If a father does not speak into his son's developing story, someone else will -- the stakes are not merely relational but formational: a young man will spend the entire summer imagining the kind of person he will become, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy for good or ill.
quotes: Fathers, you are the most significant and impactful voice in your son's life. Do not listen to anyone who says otherwise. There is a rubbish view that once your son becomes a teenager, the most influential force in his life is his peers. That is false.

Your son will spend the entire summer imagining what type of person he will become next year, and whatever he imagines about himself, he will eventually live out. He is creating a self-fulfilling prophecy, whether for good or for ill.

He needs to take a risk and share honestly where he really is. He needs to know that you are not going to judge or shame him and that what you discuss will remain between the two of you unless he gives permission for it to be shared with others.
The questions are designed to shape his imagination so that his peers, social media, and the entertainment industry do not shape it for him.
Fathers, there is no man on earth who knows your son better than you do. Your voice in his life weighs as much as an aircraft carrier.

The research is clear that for boys raised in the church, the first year after high school is crucial for faith persistence. It is a season in which fathers should lean in as guides, coaches, and sages walking alongside their sons as they make critical life decisions.
